interactive.title: Equal times, equal fractions
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: This is a short lesson in thirteen small screens, all on one plot. A capacitor C, charged to 12 V, discharges through a resistor R. The circuit is drawn small beside the plot. Voltage runs up the side, from 0 to 12 V. Time runs along the bottom, from 0 to 10 s. The parts start at R = 20 kΩ and C = 100 µF. So RC = 2 s. The current leaving the capacitor is v ÷ R. That current drains it, so C dv/dt = −v ÷ R. The rule is dv/dt = −v ÷ RC. So the voltage falls at a rate in proportion to what is left. It falls 6 V a second at 12 V, and 3 V a second at 6 V. A shaded window of fixed width sits on the curve. Readouts show the voltage at its start, the voltage at its end, and end ÷ start. A rate arrow at each end of the window shows the rule's slope there, −v ÷ RC. So the end arrow is always shallower than the start arrow by the same ratio. Because the rate is always the same share of the voltage, every window of one width keeps the same share. A 1 s window reads e^(−1/2), which is 0.607. A switch flips the sign to dy/dt = +y ÷ 2. That curve starts from 1 and runs over 0 to 4 s on its own scale. Then a 1 s window multiplies by 1.649 wherever it sits. On a phone the three readouts wrap onto two lines. Here is each screen in turn. Screen 1 shows the circuit and the rule, with rate arrows on the curve at 12 V and 6 V. Screen 2 asks the rate at 3 V. The choices are −1.5 V a second, −6 V a second or +1.5 V a second. Screen 3 lets you drag the 1 s window. Wherever it sits, end ÷ start reads 0.607, from 12 V to 7.28 V or from 2.68 V to 1.62 V. The sign switch shows growth by 1.649 in every 1 s. That is e^(1/2), so every 2 s multiplies by e. Screen 4 puts the window at 6 s, a place screen 3 never shows, and asks what end ÷ start reads. It could be the same 0.607, smaller because it is nearer zero, or larger because the curve is flatter. Screen 5 separates the rule. Dividing by v gives (1 ÷ v) dv/dt = −1 ÷ RC, to be integrated over t. Then the v terms slide to the left side and the t terms to the right. That gives dv ÷ v = −dt ÷ RC, its short form. Screen 6 asks which line separates dN/dt = −λN. The choices are dN ÷ N = −λ dt, dN = −λN dt, or N dN = −λ dt. Screen 7 integrates both sides to ln v = −t ÷ RC + c. Then v = e^(−t/RC + c), which is e^c × e^(−t/RC), or A e^(−t/RC). A family of curves for different A fans out. The start at 12 V picks one, v = 12 e^(−t/2). Screen 8 asks which curve starts at 9 V with τ = 3 s. The choices are v = 9 e^(−t/3), v = e^(−t/3) or v = 9 e^(−3t). A wrong pick is drawn so you can see its start or its pace is wrong. Screen 9 puts the answer back into the rule. A rider slides along 12 e^(−t/2). It carries two readouts, the curve's slope and −v ÷ 2. They agree everywhere. At 2 s both read −2.21 V a second. Screen 10 asks which rule y = 5 e^(−2t) solves. The choices are dy/dt = −2y, dy/dt = −y ÷ 2 or dy/dt = −10. Screen 11 makes the window one RC wide. End ÷ start then reads 0.368. Putting t = RC into 12 e^(−t/RC) gives 12 e^(−1), and e^(−1) is 0.368. A straight tangent leaves the start at the starting rate, −6 V a second. It reaches zero at 2 s. The curve is still at 4.41 V there. Then R and C sliders appear. R runs from 10 to 40 kΩ, and C from 50 to 150 µF. They stretch the curve, the tangent and the window together. So the window still reads 0.368, and the tangent still lands at one RC. Screens 12 and 13 mix it all. Screen 12 takes a coil of 0.5 H carrying 2.4 A. Its current dies round a loop through 10 Ω. It asks the current after 0.05 s. The choices are 0.883 A, 0 A or 1.52 A. Screen 13 takes dy/dt = +y ÷ 5 from 100 and asks the value after 5 s. The choices are about 272, 200 or 36.8. A reactor's power grows this way. Each puzzle offers three answers.
interactive.ignores: The parts are ideal. A real capacitor leaks a little through itself. A real resistor warms and changes slightly. The curve is drawn at once, not in real time. Near 10 s it looks as if it touches zero. By this rule it never quite does. The voltages, resistances and capacitances are example values. The growth switch has no units. No real quantity can grow this way for ever.

explain.text:
When a quantity falls at a rate in proportion to what is left, it loses the same fraction in every equal stretch of time. Its curve is y = A e^(−t/τ). The rule itself leads you there. Take a capacitor charged to v volts, discharging through a resistor R. By Ohm's law the current leaving it is v ÷ R. You already know i = C dv/dt. That current drains the capacitor, so C dv/dt = −v ÷ R. Divide both sides by C to get the rule, dv/dt = −v ÷ RC. Say R = 20 kΩ and C = 100 µF. Then RC = 2 s. At 12 V the voltage falls at 6 V a second. At 6 V it falls at 3 V a second. Half the voltage gives half the rate. A coil's current falls the same way. It dies through a resistor once its supply is taken away. Radioactive atoms decay exponentially too. Their rate depends on their decay constant.

That proportion is why equal times take equal fractions. The rate is always the same share of the voltage. So each second takes the same share, whatever the voltage is. Here each second keeps 0.607 of the voltage. It goes from 12 V down to 7.28 V, or from 2.68 V down to 1.62 V. The flat line v = 0 is this rule's steady state. Each second keeps a fraction of what is left. So the curve closes in on that line but never quite gets there.[^1] Flip the sign to dy/dt = +y ÷ τ, and the same reasoning gives growth. Each equal time then multiplies the amount by the same factor. In each τ that factor is e. A reactor's power grows this way. Its period is the time the power takes to change by a factor of e.[^2]

To find the curve, [[separate the variables]]. Gather every v on one side and every t on the other. Divide both sides of the rule by v. That gives (1 ÷ v) dv/dt = −1 ÷ RC. It is usually written dv ÷ v = −dt ÷ RC. That is shorthand for integrating both sides over time. It does not mean cancelling the d's. Not every rule splits like this, but this one does. For a positive v, the slope of ln v is 1 ÷ v. So integrating 1 ÷ v gives ln v. Integrating the constant −1 ÷ RC gives −t ÷ RC. Each side brings its own constant. The two join into one + c. So ln v = −t ÷ RC + c. Raising e to a power undoes ln. So v = e^(−t/RC + c). A power of a sum splits into a product. So v = e^c × e^(−t/RC). Call e^c a single letter, A. At t = 0, e^0 = 1, so v = A. So A is the start voltage. Here v = 12 e^(−t/2). Write τ for RC, and the answer is y = A e^(−t/τ). Now put it back to check. The slope of e^(kt) is k times e^(kt). Here k is −1 ÷ τ. So the slope is −y ÷ τ at every t. That is the rule you started from.

τ is the [[time constant]]. You can read it two ways. First, after each τ the amount is e^(−1) of what it was. That is 0.368. A coil's current falls to 0.368 of the preceding value in each time constant.[^3] Second, take the starting slope, −A ÷ τ. A straight line at that slope would reach zero at exactly one τ. By then the curve is only down to 0.368 of its start. For a capacitor τ = RC, in seconds. For a coil τ = L ÷ R.[^4]

**A rate in proportion to what is left separates and integrates to y = A e^(−t/τ). A is the start and τ is the time constant. In every τ it loses 0.632 of what remains.[^1]**

analogy.text: Send a signal down a long cable. Each kilometre keeps the same fraction of its power. That is why a cable's loss is quoted in decibels per kilometre. Equal lengths take equal fractions, just as equal times do here. Double the length and the fraction kept is squared. So the loss in decibels doubles.
analogy.breaks: The cable's loss runs over distance, not time. Nothing in it is stored and let go. Its loss per kilometre also changes with frequency. So a sharp pulse spreads out as it travels. A discharge has one rate, so its curve keeps one shape.

practice.text:
**Safe way first:** by this rule, a capacitor's voltage never quite reaches zero. Prove it dead with an approved tester before you touch it.

- Check the rate is in proportion to the amount. Write it as dy/dt = −y ÷ τ.
- Separate. Put every y on the left and every t on the right. That gives dy ÷ y = −dt ÷ τ.
- Integrate both sides, with one + c. That gives ln y = −t ÷ τ + c.
- Undo the ln to get y = A e^(−t/τ).
- Use the start value. A is the amount at t = 0.
- Put it back to check. The slope of A e^(−t/τ) is −1 ÷ τ times itself. So both sides agree.
- Check the units. τ must come out in seconds.

**Rule of thumb:** each τ keeps 0.368 of what was there. A tangent at the starting rate reaches zero at one τ.

**Worked example:** a 470 µF capacitor at 20 V discharges through 10 kΩ. τ = RC = 10 kΩ × 470 µF = 4.7 s. So v = 20 e^(−t/4.7). Its starting rate is −20 ÷ 4.7 = −4.26 V a second. After 4.7 s it is at 20 × 0.368 = 7.36 V. After 9.4 s it is at 20 e^(−2) = 2.71 V.

**Common mistakes**
- Separating wrongly. dN = −λN dt still has N on both sides. Divide by N first.
- Leaving out the + c. Then A is 1. The curve starts at 1 instead of at its start value.
- Turning τ upside down. y = 5 e^(−2t) has τ = 0.5 s, not 2 s.
- Reading τ as the time to empty. After one τ, 0.368 of the start is still there.
- Holding on to the starting rate. The rate shrinks with the amount. So the fall slows.
